plain_english: I think the old teacher should be sitting here working on a different problem. Not figuring out how to keep you from having low thoughts or talking badly about yourselves. Instead, he should make sure none of you young people get the wrong idea. Here's what I mean: you'll learn that you're related to God. You'll see that we're chained down by our bodies and possessions and all the stuff we need to get by in life. But don't think this means you should throw it all off like it's some painful burden you can't stand. Don't think you should just leave everything behind to go be with your divine family. That's the real work your teacher should be doing — if he's actually doing his job right.
original_excerpt: I indeed think that the old man ought to be sitting here, not to contrive how you may have no mean thoughts nor mean and ignoble talk about yourselves, but to take care that there be not among us any young men of such a mind, that when they have recognized their kinship to God, and that we are fettered by these bonds, the body, I mean, and its possessions, and whatever else on account of them is necessary to us for the economy and commerce of life, they should intend to throw off these things as if they were burdens painful and intolerable, and to depart to their kinsmen. But this is the labor that your teacher and instructor ought to be employed upon, if he really were what he should be.
source_reference: Discourses, How from the Fact That We Are Akin to God a Man May Proceed to the Consequences, Section 1

plain_english: You should come to him and say: Epictetus, we can't stand being tied to this weak body anymore. We're tired of feeding it, giving it water and rest, keeping it clean. We're tired of doing what others want just because of this body. Aren't these things meaningless to us? Isn't death harmless? Aren't we related to God? Didn't we come from him? Let us go back where we came from. Let us finally break free from these chains that bind us and weigh us down. This world has robbers and thieves and courts and tyrants. They think they have power over us through our bodies and our stuff. Let us show them they have no power over anyone.
original_excerpt: You should come to him and say: Epictetus, we can no longer endure being bound to this poor body, and feeding it, and giving it drink and rest, and cleaning it, and for the sake of the body complying with the wishes of these and of those. Are not these things indifferent and nothing to us; and is not death no evil? And are we not in a manner kinsmen of God, and did we not come from him? Allow us to depart to the place from which we came; allow us to be released at last from these bonds by which we are bound and weighed down. Here there are robbers and thieves and courts of justice, and those who are named tyrants, and think that they have some power over us by means of the body and its possessions. Permit us to show them that they have no power over any man.
source_reference: Discourses, How from the Fact That We Are Akin to God a Man May Proceed to the Consequences, Section 1

plain_english: I would tell them: Friends, wait for God. When he gives the signal and releases you from this duty, then go to him. But for now, endure living in this place where he has stationed you. This time you spend here is short and easy to bear if you have the right attitude. What tyrant, thief, or court can frighten someone who considers their body and possessions worthless? So wait. Don't leave without good reason.
original_excerpt: And I on my part would say: Friends, wait for God: when he shall give the signal and release you from this service, then go to him; but for the present endure to dwell in this place where he has put you. Short indeed is this time of your dwelling here, and easy to bear for those who are so disposed; for what tyrant, or what thief, or what courts of justice are formidable to those who have thus considered as things of no value the body and the possessions of the body? Wait then, do not depart without a reason.
source_reference: Discourses, How from the Fact That We Are Akin to God a Man May Proceed to the Consequences, Section 1
